children: Canadian capital spending may have picked up recently after no growth in the decade through 2024, but it is still on the sluggish side and has plenty of room to recover, Bank of Montreal's Douglas Porter says. Capital spending has typically risen and fallen in sync with the economy, but since 2001 has been wildly out of sync, the economist says. First it ran much stronger than overall growth, then much weaker than GDP. Porter says the experience from the early 2000s may suggest that not all investment necessarily is efficient, which could have played a role in the capital spending drought since 2015.
